extracted.intended_audience: laboratory technicians, medical/microbiology students, and bacteriology practitioners preparing culture media
extracted.subtask_description: Step-by-step laboratory procedures and quality controls for preparing a wide range of bacteriological culture media (bouillons, gelatines, agars, blood/serum/media for special purposes), including sterilisation, pH control, clarification, filtration, tubing and incubation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discontinuous sterilisation routine (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine method of exposure in the steam steriliser at 100 deg. C. (without pressure) for twenty minutes on each of three successive days for all fluid media, and thirty minutes on each of three successive days for all liquefiable or solid media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the default sterilisation regime; only when departing from these general rules are further details given. (Repeated throughout the chapter for specific media.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use live steam at 100°C to dissolve gelatine/agar
rubrics_metrics.description: Bubble live steam (at 100 deg. C.) through the medium mass to effect complete solution of gelatine or agar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical durations: gelatine—steam ~10 minutes; agar—steam ~25 minutes (times vary by medium and are stated in each recipe). The steam can arrangement (steam can with safety and delivery tubes reaching the medium flask) is specified to achieve this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for condensation when preparing gelatine (double strength meat extract)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use double strength meat extract for gelatine because steam condensation in the medium flask during steaming will add water; the double strength compensates for this loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote explanation and example weights are provided (e.g., 1115 g total before filtration; average after filtration ~1080 g). Modify figures if ingredient percentages change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing and making up to exact volume by balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Weigh the flask and contents, compute the water required to make up the bulk to 1 litre, and add boiling distilled water from a wash bottle until the trip balance pans are exactly balanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: in one pan place the counterpoise and calculated medium weight; in the opposite pan place the flask containing the medium mass; add boiling distilled water until balance is achieved — ensures accurate final volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titrate and adjust reaction (pH) to specified value
rubrics_metrics.description: Titrate and estimate the reaction of the medium mass; calculate and add the amount of soda (sodium hydroxide) solution required to set the reaction to the specified value (often +10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control the titration result and then heat (e.g., in steamer at 100°C for 20 minutes) to precipitate phosphates after alkali addition. Many recipes specify the target reaction (e.g., nutrient bouillon +10; Nutrose medium standardised to +2.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify media with egg white
rubrics_metrics.description: Whip the whites of eggs, add to the medium at ~60°C, heat until egg-albumen coagulates forming firm masses, then filter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical: add whites of two eggs to 1 litre medium, steam until coagulated (times vary — e.g., ~30 minutes for some media, 1 hour for agar), then filter through papier Chardin into sterile flask. Clarification may require longer steaming for some formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter through appropriate filter (papier Chardin or Swedish paper)
rubrics_metrics.description: Filter clarified media through papier Chardin (or Swedish filter paper where specified) into sterile flasks before tubing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a hot-water funnel for viscous media (e.g., agar). If filtrate remains cloudy, further filtration through porcelain candles may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tube specified aliquots and cap appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Fill media into sterile tubes (commonly 10 c.c. or 15 c.c. per tube) or flasks as specified by the recipe, and cap or plug suitably (cotton-wool, india-rubber caps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some media note specific tube volumes (10 or 15 c.c.); potato wedges are placed on cotton-wool and plugged with cotton. To prevent drying, glycerine bouillon additions may be made between solidifying and incubating steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incubate filled tubes to detect contamination and discard contaminated tubes
rubrics_metrics.description: Place tubes of filled and sterilised media in the incubator at 37 deg. C. for 48 hours in order to eliminate/identify any that have been contaminated; discard contaminated tubes and store remainder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This quality-control incubation is specified for many media (blood-serum, egg medium, milk, potato tubes, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat treatment schedule for blood-serum (inspissated)
rubrics_metrics.description: After collecting and separating serum: heat tubes containing serum to 56 deg. C. in a water-bath for half an hour on each of two successive days; on the third day heat in an inspissator to about 72 deg. C. to coagulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At ~72°C a fairly transparent coagulum forms; above 72°C a thick turbid coagulum forms. After inspissation, incubate 37°C for 48 hours to detect contamination. An alternative fractional sterilisation: 56°C for 30 minutes on six consecutive days, store fluid and coagulate when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of serum water (dilution and sterilisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For serum water, mix 100 c.c. serum with 300 c.c. distilled water (1:3), steam at 100 deg. C for 30 minutes, filter if turbid, and if storing, complete sterilisation with two subsequent steamings at 100 deg. C for 20 minutes at 24 hour intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This destroys diastatic ferment and partially sterilises; subsequent steamings ensure complete sterilisation for storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citrated blood collection and incorporation into agar
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect blood aseptically from a seared heart into a flask containing sterile glass beads and concentrated sodium citrate, agitate, then add 1 c.c. citrated blood to each tube of liquefied agar (cooled to 42°C), rotate to diffuse blood, set slanted, incubate and eliminate contaminated tubes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps include sterilisation of instruments, searing left ventricle surface, use of sterile capillary pipette, and rotation of tubes between hands to distribute blood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milk media: heat-treatment, acidity limits, and rejection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat 1 litre fresh cow's/goat's milk in steamer at 100 deg. C for one hour; measure reaction (normal cows' milk averages +17). Reject milk if acidity > +20 or < +10 or if antiseptics have been added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After cooling and skimming, draw off fat-free milk into sterile tubes (10 c.c.), sterilise at 100°C for 20 minutes on five successive days, incubate 37°C for 48 hours to detect contamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potato tube preparation and instrument material precaution
rubrics_metrics.description: Use large potatoes, wash, peel, core cylinders with apple-corer (~1.4 cm), cut oblique wedges, optionally soak in 1% sodium carbonate 30 minutes to raise reaction to +10, insert on sterilised cotton-wool in tubes and sterilise 100°C for 20 minutes on five consecutive days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: cork borers and knives should be silver or silver-plated to prevent discoloration of potato wedges (steel causes discoloration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wort preparation and preservation of natural reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare wort from crushed malt and water (macerate, strain, steam), filter and sterilise; the natural reaction of the wort should not be interfered with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unhopped wort may be obtained from breweries, diluted 1:1 with distilled water, steamed and sterilised as necessary. Hopped wort is toxic to many bacteria including lactic acid bacteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dextrose (sugar) media: composition, litmus indicator, and sterilisation cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare dextrose solution of peptone (20 g) and glucose (10 g) per litre, steam 20 minutes to dissolve, add Kubel-Tiemann litmus 50 c.c., fill tubes with Durham gas tubes, and sterilise at 100°C for 20 minutes on each of three consecutive days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not sterilise sugar media in the autoclave (temperatures above 100°C induce hydrolytic changes). Do not exceed the 20-minute sterilisation period to avoid discolouring the litmus or producing yellow tints when inoculated with acid-forming bacteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral litmus solution preparation and neutralisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare neutral litmus by alcohol extraction of commercial litmus, drying, macerating in water, acidifying with sulphuric acid until wine-red, precipitating with excess baryta to alkaline, bubbling CO2 until definitely acid, then sterilising (100°C for 30 minutes on each of three consecutive days) to drive off CO2 and leave the solution neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kubel-Tiemann litmus (Kahlbaum) is recommended as most satisfactory; the in-lab preparation is lengthy and requires care.

rubrics_metrics.name: MacConkey (Bile Salt) broth composition and litmus tinting
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare bile salt broth by emulsifying Witte's peptone (20 g) with warmed water, adding sodium taurocholate (5 g) and glucose (5 g), dilute to 1000 c.c., steam 20 minutes, filter, add sterile litmus to colour the medium deep purple (about 13% required), tube into 10 c.c. with small gas tubes and sterilise 100°C for 20 minutes on each of three successive days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This medium is classed among those used for anaerobic/intestinal bacteria; recipe specifies percentage litmus to reach deep purple tint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of glucose-formate media (Kitasato) and sulphindigotate media (Weyl)
rubrics_metrics.description: To nutrient bouillon or gelatine add glucose (2%) and sodium formate (0.4%) for glucose formate media; for sulphindigotate media add glucose (2%) and sodium sulphindigotate (0.1%). Tube and sterilise as for respective base medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sulphindigotate media are blue and are decolourised to light yellow during growth of anaerobic bacteria; recipes follow base nutrient media instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inosite-free bouillon verification by test-cultures
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare bouillon, inoculate with B. lactis aerogenes and incubate to consume sugars, heat, then inoculate with B. coli communis and repeat heating and filtering until neither organism produces acid or gas — this verifies the bouillon is sugar-free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final filtration and sterilisation produce sugar-free bouillon suitable for preparing sugar media of exact composition (glucose, maltose, lactose, saccharose).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific additions for specialized media (iron, lead, nitrate etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare base nutrient bouillon (or peptone solution) and dissolve specified salts in given amounts — e.g., ferric tartrate 0.1% for iron bouillon, lead acetate 0.1% for lead bouillon, potassium nitrate 0.5% for nitrate bouillon — then tube and sterilise as for bouillon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes: alternative salts (e.g., lactate of iron) may be substituted; nitrate salt proportion can vary from 0.1 to 1% for special requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iron/lead/nitrate peptone solutions (Pakes) procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare peptone solution, fill into tubes, then add to each tube a small aliquot (e.g., 0.1 c.c.) of the neutral solution of ferric tartrate or lead acetate to produce the characteristic precipitate, then sterilise as for nutrient bouillon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: iron peptone—add 0.1 c.c. of 2% ferric tartrate (yellowish-white precipitate forms) before sterilisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litmus bouillon tinting and expected litmus response
rubrics_metrics.description: Add sufficient sterile litmus solution to tint nutrient bouillon a dark lavender; media adjusted to +10 will usually react very faintly alkaline or occasionally neutral to litmus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use litmus-tinted media for observing acid/alkaline changes during bacterial growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capaldi-Proskauer medium preparation and neutralisation to litmus
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare specified salts and asparagin/mannite additions, measure 25 c.c. and titrate against decinormal sodic hydrate using litmus; control and add sodic hydrate to render remainder neutral to litmus; filter, add litmus solution (5%) and sterilise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutralisation to litmus is an essential step before final sterilisation and adding litmus indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urine media: specific gravity and reaction restoration
rubrics_metrics.description: For urine gelatine: collect fresh urine, if specific gravity >1010 dilute with sterile water to 1010, estimate reaction at boiling-point, add gelatine (10%), heat to dissolve, then estimate reaction and add sufficient caustic soda to restore the reaction of the medium mass to the equivalent of the original urine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filter and clarify with egg as for nutrient gelatine, then tube and sterilise as for nutrient gelatine. For urine bouillon, leave reaction unaltered.
